newsitem.title: BURMA: Life goes on as normal for most in Rangoon.
newsitem.headline: Life goes on as normal for most in Rangoon.

text.p: Around democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi's house, Burma's capital could be a city under seige.

But in the rest of Rangoon on Sunday most residents appeared unaffected by a wave of detentions and the presence of heavily-armed police and military intelligence officers blocking passage to the road leading to Suu Kyi's house.
Families strolled down the city streets, street hawkers continued their loud calls and people prayed at pagodas.
Many Rangoon residents interviewed by Reuters in the city centre appeared unaware of what was going on near Suu Kyi's house, in the smart residential area on the banks of Inya Lake.
Nor did they know about the 109 members of Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) who had been detained before they could get to a three-day party congress at Suu Kyi's house on Friday.

Those who did know about the roadblocks which had been in place since early on Friday seemed more frustrated by the traffic jams they caused than concerned about the military government's efforts to prevent the meeting from taking place.
"We don't care who wins in this arm-twisting," said taxi driver Ko Tin Aung. "What we care is we can't move about conveniently. Traffic is getting heavier."

Troops were deployed on several blocks on either side of Suu Kyi's University Avenue home, diverting vehicles and pedestrians from travelling on the street. The blockage on University Avenue, a main thoroughfare, caused traffic snarl-ups for miles.
Others complained about personal inconvenience as those who lived on the street had to show proof of residence to officials before they could enter their own street.

One hotel overlooking a checkpoint was temporarily closed after officials detained several foreign journalists on Saturday in the hotel for taking pictures of the troops. The hotel later closed to avoid further problems, a former hotel guest said.
Several dozen people who had apparently come to attend a regular speech by Suu Kyi on Saturday were detained by police and put on military trucks after they refused to move away.
At least one foreigner was put on the truck then released a few minutes later after an official said he made a mistake, a witness said.

"They do this to scare us," said one old man after watching several people with their heads down getting put on the trucks. "They want to show everyone how powerful they are, so they arrest a few and scare away the others."
"And it works. We are scared," he said, shaking his head.
Foreign visitors who went near Suu Kyi's house said they were surprised by the military presence.
"If it wasn't for this situation, it would be a very nice country to visit," a British tourist in his 30s told Reuters near the checkpoint after a run-in with officials.
An American tourist in the city centre said he had heard of the problems on his arrival in Rangoon on Saturday.
"I was asking around to find out how I could go see Aung San Suu Kyi speak, but I was told this was not a very good time and I should come back a different weekend," he said.
Ever since her release from six years of house arrest in July 1995, Suu Kyi has spoken from her gate every Saturday and Sunday.
The speeches, which were intially made to a few hundred quiet listeners but have attracted up to 10,000 cheering supporters, are now a regular item on the tourist list of things to do in Burma.
